¶
'''waste-gate''' (wāst′gāt), ''n.'' A gate for letting the water of a dam or pond pass off.

'''waste-good†''' (wāst′gu̇d), ''n.'' [< ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + obj. ''good.''] A prodigal; a spendthrift.
{{smaller block|A young heyre, or cockney, that is his mothers darling, if hee haue playde the ''waste-good'' at the Innes of the Court, . . . falles in a quarrelling humor with his fortune, because she made him not king of the Indies.
{{right|''Nashe'', Pierce Penilesse, p. 18.}}}}

'''wastel†''' (wās′tel), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wastel'', < OF. ''wastel'', ''gastel'', ''gasteau'', a cake, bread, pastry, F. ''gâteau'' (Wall. ''wastiau'') (Picard ''wastel'' = Pr. ''gastal''), a cake, < MHG. ''wastel'', a cake.] '''1.''' A cake.
{{smaller block|Thow hast no good grounde to gete the with a ''wastel'', But if it were vith thi tonge or ellis with thi two hondes.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 293.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''her.'', a bearing representing a round cake.

'''wastel-bread†''' (wās′tel-bred), ''n.'' The finest quality of white bread; bread made of the finest flour.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of smale houndes had she, that she fedde
With rosted flesh, or milk, and ''wastel-breed.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 147.}}
Mysie was a dark-eyed laughter-loving wench, with cherry-cheeks, and a skin as white as her father’s finest bolted flour, out of which was made the Abbot’s own ''wastel-bread.'' {{right|''Scott'', Monastery, xiii.}}}}

'''wastel-cake†''' (wās′tel-kāk), ''n.'' Same as ''wastel.'' ''Scott.''

'''wasteless''' (wāst′les), ''a.'' [< ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] That cannot be wasted, consumed, or exhausted; inexhaustible.

'''waster<sup>1</sup>''' (wās′tėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''waster''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To waste; squander. ''Galt.'' [Scotch.]

'''waster<sup>2</sup>†''' (wās′tėr), ''n.'' [Origin obscure; cf. ''waste''<sup>3</sup>, and dial. ''wastle'', a twig.] '''1.''' A wooden sword formerly used for practice by the common people.
{{smaller block|As with wooden ''wasters'' men learn to play at the sharp, so practice in times of peace makes ready for the time of war.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 42.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''leister''. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|This chase, in which the fish is pursued and struck with barbed spears, or a sort of long-shafted trident called a ''waster'', is much practised at the mouth of the Esk, and in the other salmon rivers of Scotland.
{{right|''Scott'', Guy Mannering, xxvi.}}}}
'''To play at wasters†''', to practise fencing; fence with cudgels or with wooden or blunt swords.
{{smaller block|Thou’rt a craven, I warrant thee; thou would’st be loth to ''play'' half a dozen venies ''at wasters'' with a good fellow for a broken head.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iv. 3.}}
They that ''play at wasters'' exercise themselves by a few cudgels how to avoid an enemy’s blows.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 375.}}}}

'''wastern†''', ''n.'' [ME., var. of ''wasten'', after ''wildern''.] A waste or desert place.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ffore wolvez, and whilde sywnne, and wykkyde bestez,
Walkede in that ''wasternne'', wathes to seche.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2934.}}}}

'''wastery''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' See ''wastry''.

'''wastethrift†''' (wāst′thrift), ''n.'' [< ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + obj. ''thrift''.] A spendthrift.

{{smaller block|Thou art a ''wastethrift'', and art run away from thy master that loved thee well.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, i. 4.}}
A ''wastethrift'', a common surfeiter, and, to conclude, a beggar.
{{right|''Middleton'', Trick to Catch the Old One, ii. 1.}}}}

'''waste-trap''' (wāst′trap), ''n.'' A trap so devised as to allow surplus water to escape without permitting air to pass up in the opposite direction. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''wasteway''' (wāst′wā), ''n.'' A passage for waste water.

'''waste-weir''' (wāst′wēr), ''n.'' A cut made through the side of a canal, reservoir, etc., for carrying off surplus water.

'''waste-well''' (wāst′wel), ''n.'' See ''absorbing-well'', under ''absorb''.

'''wasting''' (wās′ting), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wastynge''; verbal n. of ''waste''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' In ''med.'', atrophy.—'''2.''' In ''stone-cutting'', the process or operation of chipping off fragments from a block of stone with a pick or point, for the purpose of reducing the faces to an approximately plane surface. Stone so worked is said to be ''wasted off''. Compare ''clowring''.

'''wasting''' (wās′ting), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Laying waste; devastating; despoiling.
{{smaller block|No time seems more likely for either than the time which followed the ''wasting'' expedition of Totilas which Prokopios records.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 345.}}}}

{{smaller block|That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of ''wasteness''. {{right|Zeph. i. 15.}}}}

'''waste-preventer''' (wāst′prē-ven″tėr), ''n.'' In ''plumbing'', a device for controlling the supply and flow of a water-tank. {{smaller|It combines an outlet-valve and a ball-valve on the inlet-pipe—a single lever operated by a chain so controlling both valves that no more water enters the tank than is drawn out.}}

'''waster<sup>1</sup>''' (wās′tėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wastour'', ''wastor'', ''wastoure'', ''wastowre'', < OF. ''wastour'', ''wastur'', ''gasteor'', ''gastour'', ''gasteur'', a waster, < ''waster'', waste: see ''waste''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' One who or that which wastes, squanders, or consumes extravagantly or uselessly; a prodigal; a squanderer.
{{smaller block|A chidestere or ''wastour'' of thy good.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 291.}}}}
{{smaller block|He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great ''waster''. {{right|Prov. xviii. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|He left a vast estate to his son, S<sup>r</sup> Francis (I thinke ten thousand pounds per annum); he lived like a hog, but his sonne John was a great ''waster''.
{{right|''Aubrey'', Lives (John Popham).}}}}
{{smaller block|Ye will think I am turned ''waster'', for I wear clean hose and shoon every day.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xxviii.}}}}
'''2†.''' A lawless, thieving vagabond.
{{smaller block|The statute of Edw. III. (an. reg. 5, c. xiv.) specifies “divers manslaughters, felonies, and robberies done by people that be called Roberdesmen, ''Wastours'', and Drawlacches.” {{right|Note to ''Piers Plowman'' (C), i. 45.}}}}
'''3.''' An excrescence in the snuff of a candle which causes it to waste: otherwise called a ''thief''.—'''4.''' That which is wasted or spoiled; an article damaged or spoiled in course of making. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In the ''industrial arts'', a vessel or other object badly cast, badly fired, or in any way defective or useless, or fit only to be remelted.}}
{{smaller block|Had I not taken these precautions, which some are apt to think too much trouble, I should have had many a ''waster''.
{{right|''G. Ede'', in Campin’s Mech. Engineering, p. 355.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') ''pl.'' Tin-plates (sheet-iron tinned) deficient in weight, or otherwise inferior in quality, and which are sorted out from the “primes.” They are used for various purposes which do not require the best quality of stock. to the tin-house; others are called ''wasters'', for which there is always a market at a reduction in price; the worst are called waster waste, and are used up for cases or sent away to Birmingham.
{{right|''W. H. Flower'', Hist. of Tin, p. 173.}}}}

{{smaller block|No time seems more likely for either than the time which followed the ''wasting'' expedition of Totilas which Prokopios records.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 345.}}}} '''2.''' Gradually reducing the bodily plumpness and strength; enfeebling; emaciating: as, a ''wasting'' disease.—'''Wasting palsy.''' {{smaller|Same as ''progressive muscular atrophy'' (which see, under ''progressive'').}}

'''wastingly''' (wās′ting-li), ''adv.'' Lavishly; extravagantly.
{{smaller block|Not to cause the trouble of making breviates by writing too riotous and ''wastingly''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.}}}}

'''wastor†''', '''wastour†''', ''n.'' Middle English forms of ''waster''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wastrel''' (wās′trel), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wastorel''; < ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er'' + ''-el'' (adj. termination as in ''gangrel'', etc.), or < ''waster''<sup>1</sup> + ''-el''.]   '''1.''' Anything cast away as spoiled in the making, or bad; waste; refuse.—'''2.''' Anything allowed to run to waste. {{smaller|Specifically — (''a'') Waste land; a common. ''Carew'', Survey of Cornwall, fol. 13. (''b'') A neglected child; a street Arab.}}
{{smaller block|The veriest waifs and ''wastrels'' of society. {{right|''Huxley'', Tech. Education.}}}}
'''3.''' A profligate. [Prov. Eng.]

'''wastry''', '''wastery''' (wās′tri, wās′tėr-i), ''n.''   [Also ''wastrie''; < ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ry'' (see ''-ery'').]   Wastefulness; prodigality. [Old Eng. and Scotch.]

'''wastry''', '''wastery''' (wās′tri, wās′tėr-i), ''a.'' Wasteful; improvident. [Obsolete or provincial.]
{{smaller block|The pope and his ''wastrye'' workers . . . were no fathers, but cruel robbers and destroyers. {{right|''Bp. Bale'', Select Works (Parker Soc.), p. 138.}}}}

'''wasty''' (wās′ti), ''a.''   [< ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Resembling cotton-waste.
{{smaller block|The wool becomes impoverished on account of the heat and dust, and is very tender, with a dry, ''wasty'' top. {{right|''U. S. Cons. Rep.'', No. lxii. (1886), p. 470.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
